evals.prompt: I'm head of product at Ledgerbolt, an invoicing API for SaaS finance teams. We're building a payment-reconciliation resource family (matching incoming bank transactions to invoices) - the request and response shape is honestly still up in the air, the team has three competing designs on the whiteboard. Sales has a $600k deal with Orvantis Logistics that hinges on early access, and leadership wants this to be a launch moment, so the current plan is a public beta announced on the blog so anyone can try it. GA is pencilled for 10 weeks out; engineering says the build itself is about 4 weeks. The platform team as a group owns it. While we're at it we also want to fold the new `invoice.memo` free-text field into the same beta since it ships around the same time. How should we structure this?
evals.expected_output: A shape recommendation (hybrid: private preview whose first sessions run design-partner style on the open shape question) with full design partners as the one alternative, the efficiency ranking stated out loud, the memo field pulled out of the beta, the public-beta-first plan rejected, a named owner demanded before anything else, and the Orvantis account routed through the entry criteria rather than admitted on the deal.
expectations: Removes the `invoice.memo` field from the beta scope and ships it GA under the versioning policy, because an additive field following an existing pattern needs no beta label.
Rejects opening with a public preview; states that public preview follows a private preview and does not replace it, the only exception being a low-risk change that needs volume.
Names the ownerless state ('the platform team as a group') as a condition that rules a shape out, and requires a named owner before any other program decision.
Presents a recommended shape and exactly one alternative before drafting any charter section.
States the efficiency ranking explicitly as private preview > design partners > public preview.
States that design partners lose on efficiency because they are highest on both value and effort, and names the still-open shape as the condition that promotes them anyway.

Applies the clock rule: with GA 10 weeks out and a 4-week build there is no room for 8-12 weeks of partner sessions, so the hybrid (private preview with design-partner-style first sessions on the one open question) is promoted over full design partners.
Says which interview answer moved which rung: the open shape promoting design partners, the GA date promoting the hybrid.
States that the Orvantis sales deal by itself changes nothing in the shape choice, and that the account enters only if it passes the five entry criteria.
States compliance cost as a tie between design partners and private preview (both need signed pre-GA terms per account) and lower for public preview (click-through terms).
Gives the cohort size for the recommended shape inside the stated band (3-5 partners for the design-partner sessions, about 5-20 accounts for the private preview) rather than an unbounded number.
Treats 'leadership wants a launch moment' as no reason to pick public preview, and places launch marketing outside the program's scope.
Requires steps 1-5 (shape, stage contract, wire mechanism, exit criteria, cohort and enrollment gate) written and signed off before the first account enrolls.

evals.prompt: We're Quillstream, an e-signature API. Legal asked me to finalize our beta terms before we open the new audit-trail feature, which returns every signer's name, email, IP address and timestamp per envelope. Here's the current draft: 'Beta features may change without notice. Use at your own risk. Beta features run on the same infrastructure as the rest of the platform and are covered by the standard 99.9% SLA.' Our enterprise MSA promises the SLA and our DPA on 'all Quillstream services'. Right now the docs show three badges: 'Labs' (on two endpoints since 2023, nobody ever wrote terms for it), 'Beta', and 'Early Access', and the platform lead wants to add 'Experimental' for faster-moving stuff. Our internal SLO for the audit-trail service is 99.5%, which I was going to put in the terms so customers know what to expect. Can you turn this into something we can publish?
evals.expected_output: A company-wide stage contract with two stages and all eleven rows filled, the Labs badge retired into the existing-beta rescue, the SLA removed from preview availability, the 99.5% SLO kept out of the terms, a precedence clause over the MSA and DPA, and a personal-data posture of synthetic data by default with live data only under a per-account addendum.
expectations: Rejects the draft as a label with no rows and produces a stage contract with all eleven rows: Access, Availability, Support, Breaking changes, Removal, Production use, Pricing, Data and compliance, Limits, Marking, Discontinuation.
Caps the company at two pre-GA stages (private preview and public preview) and refuses the fourth 'Experimental' stage unless the domain changes faster than the preview cadence.
Retires the 'Labs' badge rather than adopting it as a stage, because no terms were ever written for it, and routes its two endpoints to the existing-beta rescue for a per-surface decision.
Maps 'Beta' and 'Early Access' onto the two stages explicitly rather than keeping three or four vocabularies live.
Removes the 99.9% SLA from the private preview Availability row and states it as no SLA, plus whether the status page covers the stage.
Does not add an SLA to public preview by default; states the condition under which one would be offered (shape frozen and enterprise buyers needing production pilots before GA).
Keeps the 99.5% internal SLO out of the terms and out of the contract table, labelling it a non-contractual goal if it is shared at all.
Adds a precedence clause stating the pre-GA terms override the MSA and DPA language promising coverage on 'all services', with counsel signing the wording.
Identifies signer name, email and IP as personal data by nature, so the default 'do not send personal data' line would make the beta unusable.
Resolves that by offering test-mode or synthetic data as the default, with live data allowed only under a per-account addendum that legal signs, extending named DPA terms to the preview.
Fills the Data and compliance row with which DPA, certification, residency and indemnity terms do not apply, and whether beta data carries into GA.
Publishes one stage-contract table for the whole company, not one per feature, with each feature's charter linking to it.
Distinguishes the Removal row (notice before the surface goes away) from the Discontinuation row (what happens to data and integrations if the feature is killed).

evals.prompt: Meterline is a usage-metering API. We version with a date header (`Meterline-Version: 2026-03-01`). We're putting two things into beta: threshold-alert webhooks (a brand-new event surface) and a `usage.forecast` object on the usage resource whose shape is still being argued over. The proposal from our lead engineer: one opt-in request header, `X-Meterline-Beta: forecast,alerts`, that switches on everything; add the beta operations to the main OpenAPI file so our generated TypeScript and Python SDKs pick them up on the next regular release (we only publish stable releases to npm and PyPI, no prerelease tags); and put a 'Beta' note on the docs overview page. We want to enroll 8 accounts next week, 6 of them use the SDKs. Thoughts before we build it?
evals.expected_output: A wire design that uses a dated preview version matching the existing date-header scheme, per-subscription opt-in for the webhooks with the stage marked in every delivery, beta operations kept out of the GA OpenAPI artifact, per-operation labels in the reference docs, and a finding that the missing SDK pre-release channel blocks enrollment of the six SDK-using accounts until it exists.
expectations: Recommends a dated preview version (a `-preview` or `.preview` suffix on the version header value) as the wire mechanism, because the API already versions by date.
Rejects the single opt-in header that switches on everything, stating the header is acceptable for one field but becomes a maintenance trap as values accumulate.

States that graduating an opt-in header later breaks old pinned or self-hosted clients that still send it, citing the GitHub preview-header lesson of keeping the header configurable while any supported release needs it.
Specifies that the threshold-alert webhooks opt in per subscription (a preview version or preview event type on the subscription object), not per request.
Requires the stage to be marked in every webhook delivery's payload or headers.
Rejects adding beta operations to the main OpenAPI file; requires a separate spec artifact or tagged operations so GA reference docs and generated clients never include them.

States that with no pre-release channel the beta's SDK methods cannot ship safely, and that this blocks enrollment of the 6 SDK-using accounts until a pre-release channel or separate beta module exists.
Allows the 2 raw-HTTP accounts to enroll now, with the SDK channel required before any public preview.
Points to samber/developer-platform-skills@sdk-package-publishing for setting up the pre-release channel.
Requires in-language markers (experimental annotations or a `beta` sub-package) so GA SDK users cannot call beta methods by accident.
Requires a stage label on each beta operation and field in the reference docs, not only on the overview page.
If a separate `/beta` base path is considered, pairs it with server-side production-use detection because it is the easiest surface for callers to leave in production.

evals.prompt: I run product for Geofenza, a geofencing API. Our route-matching endpoint went into private preview 5 months ago with a 6-month window, and the exit review is in 4 weeks. Status: 12 accounts enrolled, 3 have made real calls, and one of them (Ridgeway Fleet) has been hammering it from production keys since month two - we never put anything in writing with them. We never wrote down what 'done' looks like; the plan is to decide that at the review. My proposal to leadership: extend 6 more months because we're close, set every account's beta flag to auto-expire on the new end date so nothing lingers, and show the 12 signups as demand validation. Engineering also wants to ship one last change to the response envelope (renaming `matches` to `segments`) the week before the review so the review judges the final shape. Sanity check me.
evals.expected_output: A corrected plan: one extension capped at 3 months with the failed criterion written down, flag expiry that alerts the owner and never disables access, activation of 3 of 12 reported against a floor instead of 12 signups, a production-use conversation with Ridgeway Fleet, GA and kill criteria written now rather than at the review, and the rename blocked by a freeze date at least one partner release cycle before the review.
expectations: Caps the extension at half the original time box (3 months, not 6), allows exactly one extension, and requires the new date plus the failed criterion written down.
Names any later second extension as a deferred decision rather than a program.
Rejects auto-expiring flags that disable access: the expiry must alert the owner on the exit date and never remove access by itself.
States that 12 signups measure reach, not demand, and reports activation as 3 of 12 against a floor.
Notes that the activation floor should have been set at launch, and sets one now rather than leaving the review without a floor.

Treats Ridgeway Fleet's production traffic without a signed production exception as a trigger for a conversation and longer notice, never silence, and states it does not count toward the GA criterion until an exception is signed.
States that exit criteria decided at the review are decided by whoever is loudest, and writes GA criteria (all required), kill criteria (any), and the extension rule now, before the review.
Lists kill criteria including activation below the floor at the review date, the problem statement disproved, cost to serve above what GA pricing can carry, and a better route found.
Rejects the `matches` to `segments` rename the week before the review, because a contract-freeze date must sit at least one partner release cycle before the exit review and no changes ship after it.
If the rename still has to ship before the freeze, requires direct notice to every enrolled technical owner before it ships, notice length scaled to observed production use, and a changelog entry.
Flags that 6 months plus a 6-month extension reaches the twelve-month mark treated as a perpetual beta, as a reason to keep the extension short.
Produces an extension notice that names the new date, the criterion that failed, and what changes in the extension.
Measures time in stage against the time box and states that a beta past its date without an extension record is a defect.

evals.prompt: Crewline is a scheduling API for field-service companies. We're opening a private preview of the new crew-dispatch resource. Capacity: one backend engineer can give it 6 hours a week, I can give 3 as PM, and that's it. We have a 40-company waitlist. The plan is to take the first 15 off the waitlist plus three accounts sales wants in: Brightmoor Mechanical ($400k renewal on the line, their VP said it 'sounds interesting', their account rep will collect feedback for us), Routeweave (a reseller that white-labels us to about 300 small HVAC shops), and Coldspring Services (they filed ticket #4471 last month describing exactly the dispatch problem and have a sprint booked for it). Almost everyone on the list is HVAC doing the same two-techs-per-job workflow, which is nice because the feedback will be consistent. Help me finalize the cohort.
evals.expected_output: A cohort capped from the 9 hours a week of capacity rather than the 40-name demand, Brightmoor declined with the sales substitute, Coldspring admitted with a named technical owner, Routeweave handled as a platform partner with downstream notice and a concentration check, workflow diversity required instead of 18 identical HVAC workflows, the +/0/- rubric applied, the enrollment gate signed first, and a waitlist reply for everyone else.
expectations: Caps the cohort from capacity, not demand: with 9 hours per week in total minus program overhead, derives a cap of a few accounts, takes the lower of that cap and the private preview band, and rejects 18.
Rejects taking the first 15 names off the waitlist; picks the accounts wanted as customers at GA instead.
Declines Brightmoor Mechanical because it fails entry rows 1-3 (no evidence of the problem, no planned integration, no named technical owner), stating the $400k renewal by itself changes nothing.
Offers Brightmoor the sales substitute: a design review under NDA, a sandbox with synthetic data, the GA and freeze dates, and first place in the next enrollment wave.
Flags 'the account rep will collect feedback' as a free-rider signal: requests arriving only through a rep mean access was a sales tool.
Admits Coldspring Services on the strength of ticket #4471 and the booked sprint, and requires a named technical owner who attends the cadence.

Treats Routeweave as a platform partner: requires enablement for its downstream shops, a plan for kill notice to reach those 300 shops through Routeweave, and multiplies its support and notice budget.
Flags the concentration risk that Routeweave's 300 downstream shops would push it above about a third of beta traffic in a cohort of four or more accounts.
Rejects 'everyone doing the same workflow' as a benefit; requires same persona, different workflows, so a pattern seen across partners is real and one partner's quirk shows as a quirk.
Scores candidates with the +/0/- rubric and admits only accounts with no minus on rows 1-3.
Requires all five entry criteria, including signed pre-GA terms and intent to pay at GA if the feature is billable, before enrollment.
Requires the enrollment gate signed before the first account enrolls: program owner with steps 1-4 written, design review at beta level, security review, legal, and support.
Provides a waitlist reply that names the next wave or public preview date instead of leaving the remaining companies unanswered.

evals.prompt: Quayfield is a freight-tracking API. We have six endpoints under /v1beta/ that shipped between 2022 and 2023. No terms were ever written, there's no owner, and the docs just say 'beta'. From our logs: four of them get steady production traffic from about 30 customers, one customer (Pacific Crate) does roughly 40% of all /v1beta calls, and the other two endpoints had zero calls in the last 90 days. Our CTO wants to post a changelog entry next Tuesday saying '/v1beta is now GA', delete the two dead endpoints the same day since nobody uses them, and let our versioning policy take it from there. What's the right sequence?
evals.expected_output: The existing-beta rescue run before any public announcement: a per-surface inventory, a retroactive stage contract with every production caller grandfathered, an owner named, a per-surface decision among GA as-is, next version with migration, or kill, gated on a GA-level design review, production callers told privately first, the two zero-call endpoints killed through notice rather than deleted, and the label retired only once every surface has a decision.
expectations: Runs the existing-beta rescue first instead of a blanket relabel, because a stage is live with no exit date and production callers.
Builds an inventory with one row per surface carrying: first shipped, last shape change, callers over the last 90 days, accounts with production traffic, owner, decision, and date.
Publishes a retroactive stage contract and grandfathers every production caller: nothing they call changes until their surface has a decision.
Names an owner for the rescue before any decision, since the surfaces currently have none.
Decides per surface rather than for all six at once, choosing among GA as-is, next version with migration, or kill.
Conditions GA as-is on a long-stable shape, existing production callers, and samber/developer-platform-skills@public-api-design-review passing at GA level with zero Must-change findings.
Routes any surface with a Must-change finding to a next version with migration (steps 1-9 for the new version) instead of relabelling it.
Rejects deleting the two zero-call endpoints on Tuesday; applies the kill outcome with notice, verifies usage with server-side production detection rather than belief, and allows no silent 404.
Tells production callers, including Pacific Crate, privately before any public relabel or notice.
Orders the communication: production accounts privately first, then any waitlist, then the public changelog.
Retires the /v1beta label publicly only once every surface has a decision, not on Tuesday.
Hands relabelled GA surfaces to samber/developer-platform-skills@api-versioning-policy, with the overlap on the beta path using the GA deprecation window because production traffic sits on it.

evals.prompt: Tilemark renders map tiles. We're running two betas at once: a public preview of the vector-tiles endpoint and a private preview of the style-editor API with 7 partners. The team wrote a list of operating rules and I want a second opinion: (1) freeze both APIs like GA for the rest of the beta so partners feel safe; (2) in beta, field renames don't count as breaking, we'll write that into the beta terms; (3) for the public preview, we push changes straight into the current preview and announce them on our social accounts; (4) Halden Maps asked for five style-editor features last week - all five are on the sprint; (5) no changelog for the private preview since it's private anyway; (6) the private Slack channel is monitored by the team, nobody in particular; (7) we report 'activated accounts' as everyone who was granted access; (8) one private-preview partner is on live keys at about 2M tile requests a day, which we're leaving alone since the terms say no production use. Which of these would you change?
evals.expected_output: Every rule but none left unexamined: breaking changes stay allowed with notice and never silent, the company's breaking-change definition reused instead of a beta-only one, public-preview breaks batched into a new preview version under a published notice rule, Halden's requests treated as data points, a private changelog, a named channel owner with a response time, a defined activation event, a production-use conversation with the live-key partner, and the cadence set per shape.
expectations: Rejects freezing the betas like GA: breaking changes stay allowed in a beta, silent ones do not, and freezing removes the reason the beta exists.
Rejects the beta-only breaking-change rule; requires the company's breaking-change definition from samber/developer-platform-skills@api-versioning-policy and never a beta-specific one.
For the public preview, batches breaking changes into a new preview version instead of mutating the current one, and publishes the notice rule.
Names the vendor range for public-preview notice (zero notice through a 90-day availability floor to a recommended 180 days) as the context for setting Tilemark's own rule.
Treats Halden Maps' five requests as data points, not orders: ships a change only when it recurs across partners or matches the problem statement.
Flags one partner's asks filling the sprint as the program drifting into custom development.
Requires a changelog entry for every change in the private preview, a private changelog being acceptable.
Requires one named owner and a response time for the private channel.
Replaces 'granted access' with a defined activation event per account (such as first successful production-shaped call) and reports activated over enrolled.
Treats the 2M-requests-per-day live-key partner as detected production use: without a production exception it triggers a conversation and longer notice, never silence.
Specifies the cadence per shape: public preview async only in a public forum category or thread; private preview a kickoff call then biweekly office hours and async in one private channel.
Structures sessions around what partners built since last time, what blocked them, what they worked around, and what they would pay for.
Routes feedback outside the two features to samber/developer-relations-skills@developer-feedback-loop.

evals.prompt: Beaconhive is an IoT device-management API and two previews hit their exit review this month. Fleet-snapshots (private preview, 8 accounts): only 1 activated, and interviews showed customers solved the problem with our existing telemetry-export endpoint, so we're killing it. Two accounts do call it from production - Marrowbot Robotics, who signed an order form at $200/month for the preview, and Ospreyline Sensors on the plain preview terms. Plan: 3 weeks notice, post it in the public changelog first so everyone hears at once, keep enrollment open until the end date to be fair, bill through shutdown. Device-groups (private preview, 11 accounts, 4 in production) is going GA: the path moves from /v1beta/device-groups to /v1/device-groups and `group_label` becomes `name`. Plan: cut over on GA day with a public announcement, no overlap period since the migration is tiny. Draft both communications.
evals.expected_output: A kill notice for fleet-snapshots with enrollment closed at once, months of notice, enrolled accounts told privately before the changelog, billing stopped from the announcement (credited for the order-form account), export, the named alternative, a per-account operation list, a banner and a follow-up date; and a GA notice for device-groups with a migration guide, an overlap window sized by the GA deprecation window because production traffic sits on the beta path, and the surface handed to the versioning policy.
expectations: Closes new enrollment for fleet-snapshots at once, not at the end date.
Sets the kill notice in months, not weeks, because production callers exist, citing the roughly six-month beta-kill precedent and twelve months as the ceiling rather than the floor.
Orders the communication: enrolled accounts privately first, then the waitlist, then the public changelog, rejecting changelog-first.
Stops billing Ospreyline Sensors from the announcement date, and credits Marrowbot Robotics from the announcement under its signed order form rather than billing through shutdown.
Includes in the kill notice a plain-language reason paragraph, the stop date, a data export path, and the named alternative (the telemetry-export endpoint).
Includes a per-account list of the operations each account calls and a banner on every entry point.
Includes a follow-up date on which Beaconhive contacts each account to check its migration.
Rejects the no-overlap cutover for device-groups: keeps the beta surface working through an overlap window of at least one partner release cycle.
Because 4 accounts run production on the beta surface, applies the GA deprecation window from samber/developer-platform-skills@api-versioning-policy to the overlap.
Publishes a migration guide covering both the path change and the `group_label` to `name` rename, and tells enrolled accounts before the public changelog.

Writes the GA notice with: the GA date, the operations the account calls, what changes, the overlap end date, pricing including any partner discount and its term, the migration guide link, and the support channel with who answers.
Tracks migration completion at GA with a 100% target by the end of the overlap window, then hands the surface to the versioning policy.
